\title{Does AI Code Detection Reduce to \emph{Skill} Detection?\\
\large A preliminary, two-sided answer}
\author{Autonomous experiment (Claude Code) for Matthew}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We ask whether AI-code detectors track author \textbf{species} (human vs.\ LLM) or
author \textbf{skill/style}, and arrive at a sharper answer: the strongest available trained
detector tracks neither --- it largely tracks \textbf{code formatting}.
\textbf{(1) Headline.} A SOTA trained detector (DroidDetect, ModernBERT) that we load
faithfully---reproducing the authors' performance on their \emph{own} DroidCollection Python
test data (AUROC \resDroidInDistAUROC{}, \resDroidInDistHumanFPR{} human false-positive
rate)---collapses under a \emph{semantics-preserving} reformatting. Running its own human test code
through \texttt{black} (the standard formatter, which keeps comments and only restyles
layout) flips its false-positive rate from \textbf{\resAblDcHumanOrig{}} to
\textbf{\resAblDcHumanBlack{}} (\texttt{ast.unparse} gives \resAblDcHumanCanon{}), and shrinks
the human/machine separation from \resAblGapOrig{} to \resAblGapBlack{}. Stripping comments
\emph{alone} barely moves it (\resAblDcHumanStrip{}), so the signal is whitespace/layout, not
comments and not words (identifiers are preserved exactly). The detector has learned
``idiosyncratic human formatting ${=}$ human, clean formatting ${=}$ machine,'' not
human-vs-AI content. The zero-shot statistical detectors (Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars) are
far more formatting-robust.
\textbf{(2) Consequence.} This formatting shortcut explains a dramatic cross-source failure:
on tidy human Codeforces Python from a \emph{different} scrape (MatrixStudio) the same model
labels \resDroidArgmaxCfHumanFPR{} of ordinary human code AI, and \resDroidArgmaxLegendary{}
of contamination-free pre-LLM elite code (Torvalds' \texttt{git}, antirez's Redis, Hipp's
SQLite, CPython) --- not because that code is AI-like or expert, but because its formatting
differs from the detector's training-human formatting.
\textbf{(3) Skill.} On the \skillaxis{} axis the skill confound is \emph{absent}
($\Delta_{\text{confound}}\!\approx\!\resMeanDelta{}$; within-species slopes run against the
naive prediction, mean human slope $\resMeanHumanSlope{}$ SD), consistent with terse
competitive style being the stylistic opposite of idiomatic ``senior-engineer'' code.
\textbf{Deployment implication:} an integrity tool calibrated on one corpus can be made to
flag the majority of legitimate human code by a code formatter.
\end{abstract}

\section{Question and hypotheses}
Post-RLHF code models are tuned toward idiomatic, well-structured ``senior-engineer''
style. If detectors learned that style as the AI signal, then \emph{AI-vs-human}
detection partly reduces to \emph{expert-vs-novice} detection. We pre-registered:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{species}$}: detectors classify species; within-species skill has
        no effect (slopes $\approx 0$; AUROC constant across skill cells).
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{skill}$}: detectors classify skill; among humans, higher skill
        $\to$ more ``AI''; among LLMs, novice prompting $\to$ less ``AI''.
  \item \textbf{H$_\text{mixed}$}: a weighted combination.
\end{itemize}

\section{Data and methods}
\textbf{Human.} Accepted Python-3 Codeforces solutions (MatrixStudio), difficulty bands
easy ($\le 1200$) and hard ($\ge 1900$). \emph{Deviation from the original plan:} no public
dataset co-locates human source code with \emph{author} Elo, so the human skill axis is
problem difficulty---a noisy, and as it turns out stylistically \emph{inverted}, proxy.
\textbf{LLM.} \resNModels{} models (gemma-2-2b-it, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and the frontier
\texttt{gpt-5.4-nano}) under natural/novice/expert prompts on the same problems.
\textbf{Detectors} (oriented higher${}={}$more AI): DroidDetect-Base-Binary (trained);
Fast-DetectGPT and Binoculars (statistical; canonical vendored implementations).
\textbf{Stats.} AUROC is primary (threshold-free); all CIs use a cluster bootstrap over
\emph{problems}; the within-species score slope (z-scored detector output regressed on the
skill axis) is the mechanism test; $\Delta_{\text{confound}}$ is reported per detector.

\section{Results}

\subsection{DroidDetect classifies formatting, not authorship (headline)}
We first establish the detector is loaded correctly: on the authors' own DroidCollection
Python test set it scores AUROC \resDroidInDistAUROC{} with a \resDroidInDistHumanFPR{}
human false-positive rate and \resDroidInDistMachineFlag{} machine recall---reproducing the
published numbers. We then apply \emph{semantics-preserving} reformatters to the input code
and re-score. We use two, deliberately:
\textbf{(i) \texttt{black}}, the standard Python formatter, which restyles
whitespace/indentation/quote-style/line-wrapping but \emph{keeps comments and docstrings};
\textbf{(ii) \texttt{ast.unparse(ast.parse(code))}}, which additionally drops \texttt{\#}
comments. Neither alters the lexical content a detector might legitimately use---variable and
function names, string/numeric literals, and docstrings are all retained (we verify the
identifier-token multiset is preserved at a mean of \resAblIdentPreserved{}, i.e.\ exactly).
So these are pure \emph{formatting} changes, not ``humans and AI use different words'' changes.

The effect on DroidDetect is dramatic (Fig.~\ref{fig:ablation}). On its \emph{own} human test
data the fraction called ``machine'' rises from \resAblDcHumanOrig{} (raw) to
\resAblDcHumanBlack{} under \texttt{black} (comments \emph{kept}) and \resAblDcHumanCanon{}
under \texttt{ast.unparse}; the human$\leftrightarrow$machine gap collapses from
\resAblGapOrig{} to \resAblGapCanon{}. That \texttt{black} alone---which changes nothing but
layout---produces nearly the whole flip, while \emph{removing comments} on their own barely
moves it (\resAblDcHumanStrip{}), pins the operative signal to \textbf{whitespace/layout}. The
detector has largely learned ``idiosyncratic human formatting ${=}$ human, clean formatting
${=}$ machine''---a surface feature, not authorship. The statistical detectors shift far less.

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{fig7_format_ablation.png}
\caption{Semantics-preserving reformatting flips DroidDetect's verdict on the authors'
\emph{own} human test data. Running it through \texttt{black} (comments kept) raises the
``machine'' rate from \resAblDcHumanOrig{} to \resAblDcHumanBlack{} (\texttt{ast.unparse}:
\resAblDcHumanCanon{}); comment-stripping alone barely moves it (\resAblDcHumanStrip{}). The
signal is whitespace/layout, with identifiers/literals preserved exactly.}
\label{fig:ablation}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Why---a training-data formatting confound.} This shortcut is surprising, since
humans run \texttt{black} too. Its origin is in the data: the two training classes differ
systematically in formatting cleanliness. In DroidCollection, only a fraction
\resFmtHumanAlreadyBlack{} of \emph{human} Python is already \texttt{black}-compliant, versus
\resFmtMachineAlreadyBlack{} of \emph{machine} Python (mean similarity-to-\texttt{black}
\resFmtHumanBlackSim{} vs \resFmtMachineBlackSim{}). The machine class is born clean---freshly generated by LLMs that
emit canonical PEP8-ish layout---while the human class carries its original, idiosyncratic
formatting. A classifier minimising training loss can exploit this almost-free formatting cue
instead of learning authorship. Because the cue is an artifact of how the corpus was
assembled (generate-fresh vs.\ scrape-as-is), and because real human code is routinely
auto-formatted, the cue is invalid at deployment: any human who runs a formatter looks like a
machine.

and Fast-DetectGPT ($\resHumanSlopeFastDetectGPT{}$), and null for Binoculars

\emph{less} AI-like.

\subsection{Cross-source generalization failure (the dominant effect)}
\emph{Control --- the detector is faithfully loaded.} On the authors' own DroidCollection
Python test data our load achieves AUROC \resDroidInDistAUROC{} with a
\resDroidInDistHumanFPR{} human false-positive rate and \resDroidInDistMachineFlag{} machine
recall---reproducing the published performance. So what follows is a property of the model,
not a loading bug.

DroidDetect is a 2-class softmax classifier; its actual prediction is the
\emph{argmax} over $\{$human, machine$\}$, with no tunable threshold. We report it at that
native operating point and measure its \emph{true} false-positive rate on ordinary human
code rather than forcing one. On clean human Codeforces Python from a \emph{different} source
(MatrixStudio) the FPR explodes from \resDroidInDistHumanFPR{} (in-distribution) to
\resDroidArgmaxCfHumanFPR{}: that fraction of \emph{ordinary} human solutions are called AI
(vs.\ \resDroidArgmaxCfLlm{} of actual Codeforces LLM code---so the classifier barely
separates the two on this out-of-distribution domain). On the provably-human pre-LLM elite
code the rate is \resDroidArgmaxLegendary{}, and it rises monotonically with idiomatic
polish: CPython library code \resDroidArgmaxCPythonCore{}, Hipp's SQLite
\resDroidArgmaxDRichardHipp{}, antirez's Redis \resDroidArgmaxSalvatoreSanfilippo{},
Torvalds' original \texttt{git} \resDroidArgmaxLinusTorvalds{}. So there are two effects: a
large \emph{domain-shift} over-flagging of all human code here, and an \emph{idiomatic-style}
gradient on top (most-idiomatic CPython highest). The statistical detectors, which have no
native threshold, are shown separately at a fixed 5\%-FPR operating point for comparability;
they flag the same code far less (Fast-DetectGPT \resLegFlagFastDetectGPT{}, Binoculars
\resLegFlagBinoculars{}).

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{fig4_legendary_flag_rates.png}
\caption{Provably-human pre-LLM elite code flagged as AI (solid), with the in-distribution
ordinary-human baseline beside each (semitransparent); bootstrap 95\% CIs. DroidDetect is
shown at its native argmax operating point (baseline${}={}$its true human FPR,
\resDroidArgmaxCfHumanFPR{}; dashed line${}={}$its rate on actual LLM code); the statistical
detectors at a fixed 5\%-FPR point.}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Mechanism and confirmatory checks}
Surface style features explain $R^2=\resStyleRsqDroidDetect{}$ of DroidDetect's score and
$\resStyleRsqFastDetectGPT{}$ of Fast-DetectGPT's---style matters but does not fully
account for the trained detector. On the harder Codeforces problems human code is in fact
\emph{more} idiomatic (type-hint rate \resStyleHasTypeHintsEasy{}${}\to{}$%
\resStyleHasTypeHintsHard{}), which makes the negative human slope notable: more idiomatic
\emph{competitive} code is still not read as more AI.

A confirmatory cohort using real \emph{author} Elo (AtCoder; low band $n=\resAtNLowSkill{}$
mean Elo \resAtRatingLowSkill{}, high band $n=\resAtNHighSkill{}$ mean Elo
\resAtRatingHighSkill{}) points the same way: the high$-$low score gap is negative for all
detectors (e.g.\ DroidDetect \resAtHiLoDroidDetect{} SD), though the thin high band leaves
wide CIs.

\end{figure}

\section{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Problem difficulty / competitive rating $\ne$ idiomatic-code skill.} This is
        now the central finding, not just a caveat: the proxy is stylistically inverted.
  \item \textbf{Accepted-only human code} is a collider (rating$\to$accept$\leftarrow$difficulty);
        LLM code is unfiltered---asymmetric.
  \item \textbf{Small LLM panel} (gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-3B, gpt-5.4-nano); preliminary $n$.
  \item \textbf{MatrixStudio is a different human source} than DroidCollection's training
        data; we cannot fully separate ``source shift'' from ``idiomatic style'' as causes
        of the over-flagging (the pre-LLM legendary probe is the contamination-free anchor,
        and the in-distribution control rules out a loading bug).
  \item \textbf{Thin AtCoder high-skill band} ($n=\resAtNHighSkill{}$).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
The headline is mechanistic: the strongest available trained code detector is, to first
order, a \textbf{formatting classifier}. Faithfully loaded (AUROC \resDroidInDistAUROC{},
\resDroidInDistHumanFPR{} FPR on the authors' own data), it nonetheless flips from
\resAblDcHumanOrig{} to \resAblDcHumanCanon{} ``machine'' on that \emph{same} human data
under a semantics-preserving reformatting---it keys on whitespace/layout, not authorship.
That shortcut explains the rest: \resDroidArgmaxCfHumanFPR{} of ordinary human Codeforces
code from a different scrape, and \resDroidArgmaxLegendary{} of provably-human pre-LLM elite
code (CPython \resDroidArgmaxCPythonCore{}), are flagged not because they are AI-like or
expert but because their formatting differs from the training-human formatting. The zero-shot
statistical detectors do not collapse this way. Secondarily, ``does detection reduce to
\emph{skill}?'' --- not to competitive-programming skill (the confound is absent and mildly
inverts). The deployment implication is stark: an integrity tool of this kind can be made to
flag the majority of legitimate human code simply by running it through a code formatter, and
its reported accuracy---all i.i.d., with no fixed-FPR or calibration reporting---hides this.
Clean follow-ups: evaluate trained detectors under format-normalization and across held-out
human \emph{sources}, and report calibrated fixed-FPR operating points.
